place.en: Foot of Mount Meng · Shi'ao village

setup.zh: 蒙山脚下的石坳村，十七户人家，一户打猎——你家。屋顶漏雨，米缸半年见底；山，是马家的。
setup.en: Shi'ao village at the foot of Mount Meng: seventeen households, one of them hunters — yours. The roof leaks, the rice jar is empty half the year; the mountain belongs to the Mas.

recap.zh: 石坳村，猎户家的孩子：爹老实，娘心细，山是马家的。
recap.en: Shi'ao village, a hunter's child: an honest father, a clever mother, and a mountain that belongs to the Mas.

zh: 十七户人家，十六户种地，一户打猎。
屋顶三年没换茅草，一下雨，盆碗齐响。
en: Shi'ao village, at the foot of Mount Meng.
Seventeen households: sixteen farm, one hunts.
Three years on the same thatch; when it rains, every bowl rings.

story.zh:
早年间，蒙山脚下有个少年，命苦到什么地步？镇上的说书先生讲他的故事，讲不到一半自己先哭了，只好把茶钱一文一文退给听众。

打那以后，说书先生再也不肯讲，倒不是不忍心，实在是赔不起。

这个少年，姓沈，名小满，这一年十二岁，生得精瘦，一双眼睛黑亮黑亮的，家住蒙山脚下石坳村。若问他是做什么的，是猎户家的独子；若问他有什么特长，只有一样：饿。

这一年秋天，他家墙上那张弓，眼看便要姓马了。

那天一早，小满是给盆吵醒的。头天夜里下过一场雨，下得不大，却下得很有耐心，一直下到五更天。

他娘已经在挨个儿倒盆了。她是个瘦小的妇人，头发挽得一丝不乱，身上的补丁一块挨一块，都补得方方正正。她倒一个，数一个：「一、二、三……」数到灶台底下那个，是「九」；数到他爹炕头那个，是「十三」；数到挂兽皮那间屋的门槛里头，是「十七」。十七个盆，一个不少。

他娘直起腰来，望着墙角那半缸雨水，道：「接了半缸。够洗三回衣裳，省两趟挑水。这场雨，不算白下。」

石坳村统共十七户人家，十六户种地，一户打猎，打猎的那一户便是沈家。村里人提起沈家，都要竖起大拇指，赞一声：「猎户家，那是祖传的手艺。」赞完了，再把大拇指慢慢收回去，补上一句：「祖传的穷。」

沈家两间房，一间住人，一间挂兽皮，到得下雨天，两间都住水。小满的娘说，咱家这屋顶是蒙山最有学问的屋顶，它知道雨从哪来，还知道雨往哪去。小满的爹说，这叫**天人合一**。他娘说：「你再合一次试试。」

他爹便不说话了。

这人最懂得什么时候不说话，这是他一辈子最大的本事，也是唯一的本事——哦不，还有一样，是他的左膝盖。

他爹是个黑瘦的高个子，背有点驼，站着像一张拉久了、松不回去的弓。这左膝盖，年轻时给野猪顶过一回，从此阴天疼，下雨疼，刮风疼，马家来收租之前，也疼，比村口那面铜锣还准。

那天一早，它便疼个不停，他爹揉一下，皱一下眉。他娘瞧了他一眼，问道：「它今儿说什么了？」他爹认认真真地想了一想，老老实实地道：「它说……今儿怕是有客。」

他娘便不作声了。

蒙山是马家的，至少马家自己是这么说的：满山的树姓马，满山的兔子也姓马。村里人砍一担柴，得交马家一捆；沈家打着的野物，一半归马家：打两只兔子，交一只；打一只獐子，交半扇。

有一年小满他爹喝了二两酒，壮起胆子，小声问了一句：「那山上的风，也姓马吗？」第二天，马家便开始收「山风钱」了。从那以后，他爹再也不喝酒了。

沈家一年到头，最常来的客只有一位，这位客从不空手来——手里总拎着那根短棍；也从不空手走。
story.en:
Long ago, at the foot of Mount Meng, there was a boy — and how hard was his lot? The storyteller in town would burst into tears before he was halfway through his tale, and have to hand the tea money back to his listeners, coin by coin.

After that the storyteller refused ever to tell it again; not because he couldn't bear to, but because he couldn't afford to.

The boy was surnamed Shen, given name Xiaoman, twelve that year, wiry and thin, with eyes bright and black, living in Shi'ao Village at the foot of Mount Meng. Ask what he did: he was a hunter's only son. Ask his special talent: there was only one. Hunger.

That autumn, the bow on his family's wall looked set to take the name Ma.

That morning Xiaoman was woken by the basins. It had rained the night before — not hard, but very patiently, all the way to the fifth watch.

His mother was already emptying the basins one by one. She was a slight woman, her hair pinned up without a strand astray, the patches on her clothes set one beside another, every one sewn square. She counted as she went: "One, two, three…" The one under the stove was "nine"; the one at the head of his father's kang was "thirteen"; the one just inside the threshold of the hide room was "seventeen". Seventeen basins, not one missing.

His mother straightened up, looked at the half-vat of rainwater in the corner, and said, "Half a vat. Enough to wash clothes three times, and two trips to the well saved. This rain didn't fall for nothing."

Shi'ao Village had seventeen households all told — sixteen that farmed and one that hunted, and the one that hunted was the Shens. Whenever the villagers spoke of the Shens they'd raise a thumb: "A hunting family — the craft's handed down." Then they'd slowly fold the thumb back in and add: "So's the poverty."

The Shens had two rooms, one to live in and one to hang the hides, and when it rained both were full of water. Xiaoman's mother said theirs was the most learned roof on Mount Meng: it knew where the rain came from, and where it went. Xiaoman's father said this was called **Heaven and man as one**. His mother said, "Go on, be one with it again."

His father said no more.

The man knew better than anyone when not to speak; it was the greatest skill of his life, and the only one — oh, no, there was one more: his left knee.

His father was a tall, dark, lean man with a slight stoop, who stood like a bow drawn too long to spring back straight. That left knee had been gored by a wild boar when he was young, and ever since it hurt when it clouded over, hurt when it rained, hurt when the wind blew, and hurt before the Ma family came for the rent — more reliable than the gong at the village gate.

That morning it wouldn't stop aching; his father rubbed it, and frowned, and rubbed it again. His mother glanced at him. "What's it saying today?" His father gave it serious thought and answered honestly: "It says… we may have a guest today."

His mother said nothing more.

Mount Meng belonged to the Ma family — or so the Ma family said: every tree on the mountain was named Ma, and every hare was named Ma too. A villager who cut a load of firewood owed the Mas one bundle; whatever the Shens hunted, half went to the Mas: two hares shot, one handed over; one river deer, half of it.

One year Xiaoman's father drank two ounces of wine, screwed up his courage and asked, very quietly: "The wind on the mountain — is that named Ma too?" The next day the Ma family began collecting "mountain-wind money." His father never drank again.

All year round the Shens had only one regular guest, and this guest never came empty-handed — he always carried that club — and never left empty-handed either.

exits.means: goes on to the evening 马三 comes for the rent — the hero is 沈小满, fixed (2026-09-30), so there is no name card
